claims.text: Formation of a uniform single-phase noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticle is governed by kinetic competition between atomic diffusion and nucleation.
A slower thermal cycle provides sufficient time for constituent atoms to intermix.
Increased intermixing during a slower thermal cycle permits configurational-entropy stabilization of a single-phase alloy.
Rapid heating and cooling trap the alloy in a metastable, heterogeneous state.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles often exhibit phase separation.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles often exhibit elemental segregation.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles often exhibit uncontrolled or irregular particle morphology.
The controlled intervention is to reduce the heating rate and introduce an intermediate dwell while holding overall composition fixed.
The intervention is applicable when atomic-size differences and enthalpy disparities among the constituent noble metals are moderate enough to permit entropy stabilization.
The relative rates of atomic diffusion and nucleation determine whether the system reaches a thermodynamically favored single-phase structure.
A slower thermal cycle allows atoms to overcome kinetic barriers and diffuse more uniformly.
Uniform diffusion allows high configurational entropy to favor a single-phase solid solution over phase separation or elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, slower processing with an intermediate dwell will increase single-phase formation.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, slower processing with an intermediate dwell will reduce compositional inhomogeneity and elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid heating and cooling, slower processing with an intermediate dwell will produce more controlled particle morphology.
Extreme atomic-size or enthalpy disparities may cause phase separation despite slower processing.
